research_text:
## 1. API and reported value

`TrustManagerFactory` creates trust managers from trust material held in a `KeyStore` and/or provider-specific sources. The reported API event is `init(KeyStore)` with a **null `KeyStore` argument**. The Java API permits null; it does not, by itself, specify that every provider must load the same platform trust store. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html?utm_source=openai))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html

For Oracle’s **SunJSSE PKIX and SunX509** factories, the JSSE guide documents a default-trust-material search for that null argument: the configured `javax.net.ssl.trustStore`, or, if the property is absent, `jssecacerts` followed by `cacerts`. If the property names a nonexistent file, the guide says an empty keystore is used. This search order is provider-specific documentation, not a universal guarantee. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

The detector’s phrase “loading was not observed” is a **report about the analysis**, not an API statement that loading failed. The supplied description also separately claims an algorithm-allowlist violation; that is distinct from the null-`KeyStore` message.

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents obtaining a factory for a supported algorithm, initializing it with a trust source, and then obtaining its trust managers. `getTrustManagers()` throws `IllegalStateException` if the factory has not been initialized. `PKIX` is required by Java SE; `getDefaultAlgorithm()` instead returns the configured or implementation-specific default. A provider-specific `ManagerFactoryParameters` implementation is another documented initialization path. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html?utm_source=openai))

Null is **not documented as inherently incorrect**. Where an explicit trust source is needed, Oracle’s JSSE guide illustrates loading a keystore of trusted certificates and passing it to the factory. A keystore must be loaded before access; loading a keystore with a null input stream creates an *empty* keystore, which is different from passing a null keystore to the factory. These sources do not prescribe a universal remediation for this detector finding. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

Certificate validation and hostname verification are separate concerns. Oracle notes that raw `SSLSocket` and `SSLEngine` use requires peer-identity checking; HTTPS hostname verification should not be disabled. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/10/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.htm?utm_source=openai))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/10/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.htm

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted formats:** Changing the factory’s trust source does not itself require converting a keystore. If a format change is independently required, Oracle documents `keytool -importkeystore` for importing entries between keystore types. Oracle documents PKCS12 as the default and recommended JDK keystore format since JDK 9. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/specs/man/keytool.html?utm_source=openai))  
  Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/15/docs/specs/man/keytool.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html
- **Wire formats:** The cited factory API does not specify a wire-format migration for changing its initialization. Changing trust anchors or validation policy can nevertheless change which peer certificates are accepted; compatibility with particular peers requires separate verification.
- **Platform support:** Java SE documents this class since 1.4 and requires `PKIX`. Android documents the class and `PKIX` from API level 1. The cited Android documentation does not establish `SunX509` as universally available. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html?utm_source=openai))  
  Source: https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory

## 4. Published CrySL rule

The linked source declares `SPEC javax.net.ssl.TrustManagerFactory`. Its matching event clauses are, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))

```text
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(keyStore);
	i2: init(params);
	Init := i1 | i2;

	gtm1: trustManager = getTrustManagers();
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl

The source declares the `getInstance` forms with one or two arguments, `init` forms using the declared `KeyStore` or `ManagerFactoryParameters` objects, and a zero-argument `getTrustManagers` form. Its order is `Get, Init, GetTrustMng?`. Its explicit value constraint requires `algorithm` to be either `"PKIX"` or `"SunX509"`; its `REQUIRES` section names `generatedKeyStore[keyStore]` and `generatedManagerFactoryParameters[params]`. It contains **no explicit null test or “loading was not observed” condition**. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/TrustManagerFactory.crysl))

**Namesakes:** No—the rule does not declare an arbitrary, name-only receiver match; it scopes the events to the specified `TrustManagerFactory` API. The rule file alone does not document how a particular analysis engine resolves receiver types, aliases, or overloads, so it cannot establish how that engine handles every namesake call.

**Source limits:** The URL points to a moving `master` branch. The supplied SHA-256 and the detector’s compiled rule revision were not independently verified here; the published rule therefore cannot be assumed to be the exact artifact that produced the report.
